title: Telephone Etiquette and Identifying Urgent Calls

sections.learningObjectives:
- Demonstrate professional telephone etiquette when answering, holding, transferring, and ending calls.
- Identify urgent calls that require immediate clinical attention or emergency escalation.
- Route calls appropriately to scheduling, billing, clinical staff, or emergency services.
- Protect patient privacy and verify caller identity when handling health information by phone.
- Document telephone messages and urgent-call escalations accurately and completely.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Picking up the phone quickly is like answering the front door right away so a guest does not walk away thinking nobody is home.

### Question 2

The greeting is like introducing yourself at the door: you say who you are and where they have called, then offer to help.

### Question 3

It is like putting a happy face in your voice; even when someone cannot see you, they can hear whether you are friendly.

### Question 4

Speaking on the phone is like reading a story aloud: not too fast, not too quiet, just clear enough for the listener to follow.

### Question 5

It is like writing your name and number at the top of a note so someone can call you back if you get cut off.

### Question 6

A good message is like a complete note to a friend: it says who called, when, why, and how to call back.

### Question 7

It is like asking a guest, "May I step away for a moment?" before you leave the room.

### Question 8

It is like only giving a locker combination to the person who can prove the locker is theirs, so their private things stay private.

### Question 9

A voicemail greeting is like a sign on a closed door that says where you are and when you will be back.

### Question 10

It is like talking with food in your mouth at the dinner table; it is hard to understand and not polite.

### Question 11

Using someone's name and saying please and thank you is like remembering a friend's name and being polite when you ask a favor.

### Question 12

Ending a call is like saying goodbye and confirming the plan before a friend leaves, so everyone knows what happens next.

### Question 13

It is like sending a question about a bill to the person who handles money, not the person who runs the tests.

### Question 14

Making an appointment is like booking a haircut; you talk to the person who keeps the calendar.

### Question 15

It is the difference between a small fire alarm that needs attention now and a reminder note that can wait until later.

### Question 16

Chest pain is like a smoke alarm; you treat it as serious right away and get help instead of waiting.

### Question 17

If a fire is burning, you call the fire department right away instead of writing a note for later.

### Question 18

A test result is like a report card that the teacher, not the hallway monitor, is the one to explain.

### Question 19

It is like making sure you copy a friend's tricky last name correctly before writing it on an envelope.

### Question 20

It is like not reading a private letter out loud in a crowded room where strangers can hear it.

### Question 21

Writing a call down is like keeping a diary of what happened so nothing important gets forgotten.

### Question 22

A refill is like asking the nurse, not the cashier, to check on your medicine.

### Question 23

A transfer is like handing a guest to a friend and saying, "This is Sam; Sam can help with your question."

### Question 24

Starting with a new patient is like signing up at the welcome desk before anything else happens.

### Question 25

Giving medical advice is like the coach deciding a play that only the doctor is trained and allowed to call.

### Question 26

It is like hearing one smoke alarm and one reminder bell at the same time; you check the smoke alarm first.

### Question 27

It is like telling a guest you will be right back, then actually coming back to check on them instead of forgetting them.

### Question 28

When someone is upset, staying calm and really listening is like pouring water on a small flame instead of adding more fuel.

### Question 29

Trouble breathing is like a car's check-engine light flashing red; you get help right away instead of waiting.

### Question 30

These warning signs are like a fire alarm for the brain; when you hear them, you call for help fast.

### Question 31

If a friend says they might hurt themselves, you stay with them and get help right away instead of leaving them alone.

### Question 32

These symptoms are like a red alert that the body needs help right now, not later.

### Question 33

If someone cannot be woken up, you call for an ambulance right away, just like calling for help when someone will not wake.

### Question 34

Serious bleeding is like a burst pipe; you shut it off and call for help right away.

### Question 35

If someone swallows something harmful, you call the poison experts right away instead of guessing what to do.

### Question 36

When you are not sure if something is a big deal, you ask a grown-up who knows, instead of guessing.

### Question 37

It is like asking what a package contains so you deliver it to the right room instead of the wrong one.

### Question 38

These symptoms are a serious warning sign in pregnancy, like an alarm that says get help now.

### Question 39

A high fever in a tiny baby is a bigger deal than in an older child, like a small engine overheating faster.

### Question 40

A seizure is like an electrical storm in the body; you call for help right away instead of waiting.

### Question 41

Results are like a private letter; you make sure the right person is asking, then hand it to the person allowed to read it.

### Question 42

Even if you do not know a person's name, you still help if they say something serious, like helping a stranger who is hurt.

### Question 43

It is like answering the fire alarm before the question about what time the office closes.

### Question 44

If the main doctor is busy, you send the patient to the next person trained to help, like a backup coach stepping in.

### Question 45

Being left on hold is like waiting at a counter while the clerk walks away and never comes back.

### Question 46

It is like not telling a stranger when your neighbor will be home; you check who is asking first.

### Question 47

It is like using a translator app to understand a note in another language instead of pretending you can read it.

### Question 48

Talking over loud music is like trying to read while someone bangs a drum; it is much easier when it is quiet.

### Question 49

It is like repeating a friend's phone number back before you hang up so you are sure you wrote it right.

### Question 50

If someone says their friend is hurt, you help the friend even though the friend is not the one on the phone.

### Question 51

A referral is like a ticket to see a specialist; you give it to the person who books those visits.

### Question 52

Medical records are like a private diary; they are only handed over through the official process and with permission.

### Question 53

It is like writing the time on a note so the reader knows how long ago it was left and how quickly to reply.

### Question 54

Sudden slurred speech is like a smoke alarm for the brain; you act on it right away.

### Question 55

Taking too much medicine is like pouring too much into a machine; you call the expert instead of guessing a fix.

### Question 56

Mild, ongoing symptoms are like a slow leak, not a burst pipe; you book a regular appointment rather than calling the emergency crew.

### Question 57

When a friend is scared, you listen and say you understand before jumping to fix things.

### Question 58

It is like serving the person who may be hurt first, then the routine questions.

### Question 59

It is like not telling a stranger about your friend's private business, even if the stranger asks nicely.

### Question 60

A voicemail is like a note on a door that anyone might read, so you keep it short and private.

### Question 61

It is like telling a guest, "I will be two minutes," before stepping away.

### Question 62

A big burn is like a serious injury that needs a doctor right away, not a home remedy.

### Question 63

If you cannot find the note about a medicine, you ask the nurse to check instead of making something up.

### Question 64

Keeping personal calls minimal is like saving your phone chats for after your shift so you can focus on your job.

### Question 65

It is like making sure your friend actually answers before you leave the room, so the guest is not left alone.

### Question 66

It is like only letting a child's parent or guardian, not any stranger, pick them up from school.

### Question 67

Speakerphone is like talking in a quiet, private room instead of a crowded hallway where anyone can hear.

### Question 68

Among all the clues, the crushing chest pain is the loudest alarm bell that needs help now.

### Question 69

Sometimes people describe a big problem with small words, like saying a fire is "just a little warm"; you still check it out.

### Question 70

A fall with a head bump and confusion is like a warning light that needs checking right away, not tomorrow.

### Question 71

These symptoms are like a low-fuel warning that needs attention now, not a month from now.

### Question 72

It is like sorting mail into the right mailboxes: emergencies to the doctor, money questions to billing, and appointments to the scheduler.

### Question 73

Losing sight suddenly is like a light switching off; you get help right away rather than waiting.

### Question 74

FAST is like a memory trick: Face, Arm, Speech, Time — remember it and act fast.

### Question 75

This is like the body sounding a full emergency alarm; you get help that very minute.

### Question 76

It is like a note that says "someone called about something"; without a name and number, you cannot call back.

### Question 77

When someone is not breathing, that is the biggest alarm of all and comes first.

### Question 78

When unsure about poison, you ask the poison experts instead of trying to guess how bad it is.

### Question 79

It is like juggling; you keep the most important ball in the air while still nodding to the next person in line.

### Question 80

If someone can barely get a word out between breaths, that is a serious alarm that needs help now.

### Question 81

Writing down the who, what, and when is like leaving a clear trail so everyone knows what happened and what was done.

### Question 82

A headache that feels like the absolute worst ever is a warning siren, not a normal headache, so you get help fast.

### Question 83

You would not promise a friend you will arrive at exactly 3:00 if you do not control the traffic; you say you will do your best and pass the message along.

### Question 84

A stiff neck with a fever and a rash is a triple alarm that says get a doctor right away.

### Question 85

If a note gets cut off halfway, you keep what you wrote and tell someone, rather than throwing it away.
